title: Carve VFM: Carving Specialists out of Generalists, Automatic Task-Specific Compression of Vision Foundation Models
abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) provide transferable visual representations, but their inference cost limits deployment in many settings. Fine-tuning specializes a VFM without shrinking it; distillation shrinks it, but through expensive teacher-guided training. Structured pruning offers a more direct route by extracting a compact subnetwork from the VFM. However, as compression gets aggressive, existing methods fail because they treat subnetwork selection and recovery as separate axes. Across layers, capacity must follow task sensitivity rather than spread uniformly. Within a layer, a removal cannot be judged by importance alone; its impact also depends on how well the lost contribution can be recovered from what remains. Selection and recovery must therefore be decided jointly. We introduce Carve VFM, which resolves this interdependence. Given a VFM, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it (i) searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers; (ii) guides the search via an adaptive recovery-aware fitness criterion; and (iii) reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into the surviving weights. The result is a dense encoder produced in minutes on a single GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four models from DINOv3 and MetaCLIP-2, Carve VFM achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations among the evaluated dense structured-pruning methods. Further fine-tuning surpasses the strongest evaluated edge model (88.1% vs. 85.8%), and carved models cut compute and memory while delivering 1.3-2.0x higher GPU throughput than the uncompressed one. These results show that the compact model you need is inside the VFM; it only has to be carved out.

title: Improved Massively Parallel Shortest Path Computation
abstract: We present new algorithms for approximate shortest path computation in weighted undirected graphs within the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model. Specifically, we construct an $a$-approximate Single-Source Shortest Path (SSSP) oracle: Given a query consisting of a source vertex $u \in V$, the oracle returns $a$-approximate distances $δ(u,v)$ for all $v \in V$. Fix an $n$-vertex weighted undirected graph. We consider two regimes of the MPC model: the near-linear regime, where each machine has $\tildeΘ(n)$ memory , and the heterogeneous regime, where all machines have $Θ(n^γ)$ memory for some constant $γ\in (0,1]$, except for a single machine with $\tildeΘ(n)$ memory . We develop randomised algorithms that construct $O(1)$-approximate SSSP oracles in $O(\log\log n)$ rounds in the near-linear regime and in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds in the heterogeneous regime. These oracles answer distance queries in $O(1)$ rounds. Our results improve upon the recent work of Dory and Matar (SPAA 2024) which, for the same total memory , requires $\left(\log\log n\right)^{2+O(1/γ)}$ rounds and applies only to unweighted graphs in the heterogeneous setting. We say that $\tilde N_k(u)$ is the approximate $k$-nearest neighbourhood of a vertex $u$ if there exists an approximate distance estimate $δ$ such that $\tilde N_k(u)$ consists of the $k$ vertices closest to $u$ according to $δ$, breaking ties by vertex ID. The main technical ingredient is a new method for efficiently computing approximate $n^{O(γ)}$-nearest neighbourhoods in the heterogeneous MPC model in $O(\log^2\log n)$ rounds.

title: About P-adic Numbers and Professor Igor Volovich on the Occasion of his 80th Anniversary
abstract: We recall a 1987 paper written by Volovich and our subsequent work with Okada which established the Feyman rules for the p-adic string and the related non-local field theory which found diverse physical applications. We add some memories of visits to Moscow during 1989-91.

title: Making LoRA Identifiable: Orthogonal Alignment for Continual Learning
abstract: There is growing interest in applying Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) to Continual Learning, as it enables faster training, mitigates catastrophic forgetting, and facilitates better adaptation to new tasks. Prior approaches have explored a range of strategies, including extending new LoRA branches for each incoming task, training under orthogonal loss objectives across all task-specific LoRA modules, and employing gating mechanisms to integrate new and existing LoRA modules. However, these methods incur memory costs that grow linearly with the number of tasks, limiting their scalability. More recent approaches investigate training a single LoRA by leveraging asymmetries in its parameterization; however, they often suffer from insufficient representational alignment across the LoRA parameter space. To address these limitations, we propose Stiefel Optimization and Aligned Rotation (SOAR), a two-stage framework for continual LoRA learning. First, we constrain the A matrix to lie on the Stiefel manifold, thereby reducing coordinate misalignment to the space of orthogonal rotation matrices. Second, we introduce an Orthogonal Procrustes alignment procedure for the B matrix to estimate the optimal rotation, coupled with a per-rank retention merging strategy that quantifies directional agreement between representations of new and previously learned tasks. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks, demonstrating that SOAR achieves strong continual learning performance without incurring additional memory overhead.

title: Compression Through Time: An Interplay of Separability, Stationarity and Capacity
abstract: Information-theoretic and geometric compression have been widely studied as possible explanations for generalization. Yet their temporal dynamics in recurrent networks remain largely unexplored. Using discretized LSTMs, whose finite embedding space enables direct estimates of information quantities, we observe pronounced compression across the final timesteps of many datasets. We explain this effect through three competing mechanisms: (i) class separability permits stronger compression at the final timestep; (ii) shared recurrent dynamics propagate this pressure across timesteps with similar activation states, making its extent depend on temporal stationarity; and (iii) limited representational capacity opposes prolonged compression because it restricts information available for subsequent computation. We systematically test these mechanisms through controlled synthetic interventions and real-world sequence tasks. Our results identify class separability, temporal stationarity, and network capacity as key determinants of temporal compression, and suggest that compression acts as a regularizer-potentially beneficial when excess capacity is available, but harmful to generalization when it consumes memory needed for the task.

title: REEL: Learning to Retrieve, Evaluate, and Evolve Visual Memory for Any Long-Horizon Multi-Shot Video Generation
abstract: Memory -based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual- memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory . Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no- memory baseline.

title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments , it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.

title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory , resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.

title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields
abstract: The martensitic transformations in stoichiometric Ni$_2$MnGa and related Heusler alloys are governed by a delicate interplay between electronic structure, magnetism, and lattice dynamics. While density functional theory (DFT) has successfully mapped the energy landscape of modulated martensites, it remains computationally prohibitive for capturing finite-temperature dynamics across relevant length and time scales. Here, we bridge this gap by constructing DFT-trained machine-learning force-fields (ML-FF) interpolated from ab initio molecular dynamics. We demonstrate that ML-FF trained on DFT data can reproduce key features of Ni$_2$MnGa, including the soft TA$_2$ phonon and a preference for nanotwinned martensites. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we explore the impact of adaptive nanotwinning on the austenite-martensite transition, which facilitates the dynamics of both, forward and backward transformation. We demonstrate, that the negative twin boundary energy along the entire transformations path predicted by DFT for $T=0$, supports the formation of ordered modulated martensites at finite temperatures. Our results pave the way for large-scale simulations of magnetic shape memory alloys with near-DFT accuracy.

title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory -Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory -efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.

title: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation
abstract: Silicon microring resonators are promising components for photonic reservoir computing because their nonlinear optical response can transform signals and retain information about recent inputs. Under constant optical excitation, their coupled free-carrier and thermal dynamics can generate self-pulsing: a periodic output response. However, constant-input behavior does not reveal how these dynamics respond to randomly modulated signals or whether their memory is useful for temporal processing. Here, we characterize a single silicon microring resonator and a passive network of microring resonators under random input modulation. The temporal component associated with self-pulsing remains observable under random modulation, but the largest fading memory occurs near the self-pulsing boundary, where no resolved self-pulsing-like oscillation is present. reservoir computing metrics, such as memory capacity, map this accessible memory , and its decay provides effective timescales associated mainly with free-carrier and thermal relaxation. Finally, we use NARMA reconstruction to test whether the measured memory profile supports nonlinear temporal processing. Responses with a resolved self-pulsing-like component perform worse on this task, and the intrinsic memory profile is not matched to the required input history. These results show that reservoir computing metrics can characterize nonlinear microring resonator dynamics even when the physical system is not an effective standalone reservoir for the selected task.

title: Spiking Neural Beamforming for Multichannel Speech Enhancement on the Edge
abstract: Speech enhancement with wearable and edge devices requires architectures that balance enhancement quality against power and memory resources. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a promising path towards this goal through sparse, event-driven computation, but existing SNN-based speech enhancement methods are largely restricted to single-channel processing and therefore cannot exploit the spatial diversity available from microphone arrays. In this work, we propose a fully SNN framework for multichannel speech enhancement based on a fully connected architecture (FC-SNN) with sequential spike encoding, derived from a compact artificial neural network (ANN) baseline via leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We characterize how enhancement performance scales with model size and spike-train length relative to ANN and classical beamforming baselines, and report the resulting parameter counts and computational complexity. We further compare direct and rate spike encoding, revealing a clear trade-off between event-driven computation and enhancement performance, and use these results to identify favorable configurations for edge devices.

title: Federated Coreset Subsampling for Distributed Memory Banks
abstract: In real-world scenarios, industrial processes can span multiple factories and goods are often produced at multiple sites, leading to a shared yet non-identical distribution of data across locations. To address this, we propose two federated approaches for i) combining existing coresets (Double Subsampling) and ii) creating new coresets (Federated Subsampling) in a distributed anomaly detection setting. In particular, we adapt the memory bank based PatchCore algorithm to a federated setting, resulting in increased cold-start performance, resilience to domain- and sensor-shift, and resilience to unreliable actor participation, a common problem in classical, network based federated learning strategies.

title: Purpose IR: Compiling User Purpose for Privacy-Preserving Agent Workflow State
abstract: LLM-agent workflows routinely transform rich observations into plans, summaries, memories, handoffs, and other reusable state. This creates a privacy boundary that task relevance alone does not capture: an observation may be needed as evidence for a task without its full semantics being authorized to persist. We call this mismatch the purpose-to-state semantic gap. The key distinction is that evidence authority is not release authority. We introduce Purpose IR, a bounded typed intermediate representation that compiles natural-language user purpose into an executable semantic boundary for reusable agent state. A Purpose program is an acyclic semantic dataflow graph in which evidence leaves specify task-required semantics, typed dependencies constrain authorized derivations, and declared sinks determine which values or actions may cross the reusable-state boundary. A deterministic compiler constructs and validates the authoritative program, while a typed runtime reconstructs reusable state only from validated sink outputs. Under explicit execution contracts, this design yields release confinement and purpose noninterference, characterizing what factual semantics may be released and which observation differences must become irrelevant to reusable state. Across 1,200 cases spanning LangGraph, CrewAI, and MobileRun, Purpose IR achieves 99.6% Privacy, 83.3% Task, and 83.3% Privacy-Compliant Success (PCS), outperforming the strongest high-privacy baseline by 27.5 PCS points. On 493 PrivacyLens trajectories, it achieves the highest Safe Action Rate at 77.3%, 10.4 points above the next-best method, extending the same boundary from reusable state to downstream actions. These results show that privacy-preserving agent state requires more than filtering sensitive or task-irrelevant content: it requires an explicit, executable representation of what the user's purpose authorizes to survive.

title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].

title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

title: BAT3R: Robust Online 3D Reconstruction with Bayesian Adaptive State Updates
abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have driven remarkable progress in 3D vision,yet their quadratic complexity renders them impractical for long video sequences. Streaming 3D reconstruction addresses this bottleneck by processing frames sequen?tially with constant memory . However, existing recurrent architectures inevitably suffer from progressive degradation over long sequences, as they fail to account for the intrinsic reliability of observations and the accumulated confidence of the historical state, leading to severe error accumulation. To address these issues, we introduce BAT3R, a training-free Bayesian adaptation framework comprising two synergistic modules: State Innovation Gating (SIG) and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU). SIG acts as a distributional regularizer that anchors state evolution to its geometric initialization, effectively arresting representational drift during long-term inference. Building on this, BASU reformulates state update as a recursive Bayesian inference process within a Kalman filtering framework. By jointly modeling the temporal reliability of observations via information-theoretic gain and spatial relevance via cross-attention maps, BASU achieves an asymmetric spatio-temporal state fusion: well-consolidated historical regions are protected from redundant updates, while genuinely novel scene content is aggressively incor?porated. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (7-Scenes, TUM, ScanNet, KITTI, etc.) demonstrate that BAT3R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online 3D reconstruction methods, with the most significant gains observed on long sequences and complex scenes.

title: Memory -Efficient Integer-Only Training of Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. Specifically, tensors are stored as signed integer mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents, on which integer-only operations are performed using five custom composable building blocks (products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinear functions, and weight updates). This allows complete implementation of trainable integer layers, including convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU. A per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across neurons and channels with diverse magnitudes. As every tensor fits in INT8, training memory is roughly 4x smaller than the FP32 baseline. We validate our training algorithm on CNNs (ResNet-18/34/50/101, MobileNetV2) and Vision Transformers (ViT-Ti / B), demonstrating for the first time that training neural networks with INT8 tensors and integer arithmetic can achieve competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at a reduced memory budget.

title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
abstract: Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension. In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements. We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/δ))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/δ))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.

title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.

title: Toward Partitioned Reference Readout for Four-Level IGZO Memory : Device Statistics, Confusion Matrices, and INT4 Error Propagation
abstract: Four-level indium-gallium-zinc oxide (IGZO) 2T0C memory needs reliable state formation, sensing references, and a path from cell errors to digital weights. We analyze 107 measured DC transfer curves from 37 isolated IGZO transistors (W/L = 3/0.5 micrometers). Four gate-bias operating points inferred from the first sweep are evaluated on later sweeps of 35 devices. Device-resolved operating points reduce second-sweep across-device current standard deviation by 49.4-52.4%, yet retaining initial thresholds increases misclassified points from 37/140 to 55/140. Leave-one-device-out reference estimation gives 0/140 on the second sweep; freezing second-sweep thresholds yields 6/140 on the third. Sampling eight reference transistors on the third sweep gives a mean held-out error fraction of 0.15% over 2,000 selections, versus 4.33% with frozen thresholds on matched held-out devices. We present conditional confusion matrices, a counterfactual common-gain sensitivity, and an INT4 error-propagation proxy. A simultaneous four-state bank with eight reference cells per state requires at least 32 physical reference cells, 12.5% of a proposed 256-cell data bank before peripheral overhead. A charge-conservation model and a partitioned hierarchical error model specify the pulse, retention, and array measurements needed to test transfer from DC device statistics to pulsed 2T0C operation.

title: HeteroVDiff: Pipelining Video Diffusion across Mobile NPU and GPU with Shared Weights
abstract: Video generation is moving from the cloud to phones for privacy and offline use, and applications often ask for several clips at a time, so on-device video generation is a throughput problem before it is a latency problem. Contemporary mobile SoCs carry both a GPU and a neural processing unit (NPU) on shared DRAM, yet existing on-device video diffusion systems run the denoiser on one engine while the other sits idle or only decodes the finished latent afterwards. Heterogeneous designs built for mobile LLMs do not carry over: they synchronise the two engines at every operator and partition weight tensors between them instead of sharing one stored copy. We first measure the platform limits that decide what can run on this class of SoC: how large one buffer may be, whether both runtimes can map the same buffer, and how much activation memory the NPU toolchain lets one graph hold. Guided by these measurements, we store the base weights once in INT8 in the layout the NPU reads natively; the GPU consumes the same bytes directly as integer dot-product operands, so neither runtime rearranges weights on load. We then flatten the denoising trajectory into its full sequence of block executions and cut it once at a block boundary, so the GPU runs the prefix and the NPU the suffix. The cut is placed from measured rather than modelled rates, including the decoder that only the NPU can run, and taken while both engines run together because each engine's speed changes when the other is active. We present HeteroVDiff, which serves a multi-expert video diffusion model across the NPU and GPU with 48% less weight memory than giving each engine its own copy. Generating videos back to back on a Galaxy S25 with decoding inside the pipeline, HeteroVDiff sustains 1.35x the stream throughput of NPU-only execution, and on VBench-2.0 it matches FP32 in the total score over all 18 dimensions.

title: Learning Rules, Memorizing Facts: An Information-Theoretic View of Hallucination
abstract: Understanding the relationship between generalization and hallucination requires clarifying the role of memorization. We study this relationship from an information-theoretic perspective through a Selector-Density Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) framework. In the sparse random-fact limit, a uniformly bounded information budget per fact forces a nonvanishing false-positive rate at recall bounded away from zero, even when all facts are observed during training. In a rules-and-facts setting, we decompose model-data mutual information into rule learning, atomic-fact memory, and excess memorization, revealing competition between rule learning and factual memory even without excess memorization. A joint budget bound quantifies the resulting constraint on atomic hallucination under perfect atomic recall. Moreover, an additive Gaussian model shows that maintaining high recall for atomic and composite facts incurs false positives even under optimal data mixing. Finally, controlled relational experiments hint how training exposure, rule complexity, and model capacity shape these trade-offs.

title: A New Lens on Multi-GPU Communication: API-Level Memory Models for Portable Optimization
abstract: As network communication increasingly becomes a performance bottleneck for ML and HPC workloads, it is more important than ever to optimize multi-GPU data transfers. Recently, low-level device APIs have emerged that allow programmers to perform fine-grain optimizations via one-sided put/get operations triggered directly from the device. However, the communication libraries providing these device APIs (e.g., rocSHMEM, MSCCL++, and NCCL/RCCL GIN) currently lack a rigorous memory model defining how their primitives interact with the underlying memory systems. Without this, emerging HPC and ML workloads aggressively optimizing network communication via device APIs can be brittle, error-prone, and face compatibility and inter-operability challenges. This paper proposes the use of API-level memory models for these emerging device communication APIs. An API-level memory model defines the memory semantics of communication API calls in a way that abstracts lower-level details from the API user and simplifies development. This work defines one such model for device-side communication (implemented in AMD's recently open sourced rocSHMEM library) and demonstrates how formal relaxations to such a model can enable low-level LLM performance optimizations while retaining a well-defined standardized interface. Specifically, we describe how updating the SHMEM API implemented by rocSHMEM can properly support cache bypassing for network data, improving performance of a collective communication workload by up to 2.48x, a fused compute+communication workload by up to 1.77x, and a state-of-the-art expert-parallel communication workload by up to 1.18x.

title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
abstract: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.

title: Recall Begets Recall: Recurrent Memory Ranking for Personalized LLMs
abstract: Memory ranking is the stage in personalized Large Language Models (LLMs) that decides which of the candidate memories returned by a retriever enter the limited context, so that the answer is grounded in the right parts of the user's history. Existing memory rankers operate in a single pass, scoring each candidate once against the raw query and cutting the ranked list at a fixed top-K. The single pass misses memories that the answer needs but that look unrelated to the query on their own, and the fixed cut ignores how many memories the query needs. To address both problems, we propose ReMind, a memory ranker that runs as a recurrent and self-terminating loop, following the cognitive theory of memory search: each recalled item joins the cue for the next recall (compound cueing), and recall stops once enough has been collected for the task (metamemory monitoring). For compound cueing, ReMind adds the top-ranked memory to the query context at each step and reranks the remaining candidates under the expanded cue, so that each recall makes the cue more specific and later steps look for what is still missing rather than for what merely resembles the query. For metamemory monitoring, a sufficiency predictor estimates at each step whether the collected memories are enough to answer the query and stops the loop once they are, so that the number of selected memories adapts to each query. Experiments on public benchmarks show that ReMind achieves the best results compared to state-of-the-art memory rankers.

title: UniSGR-V2: Stepwise Target-Side Feature Anticipation and Crossing for Generative Recommendation
abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation unifies retrieval and ranking through autoregressive decoding but differs structurally from discriminative models, which can directly access rich target-item side features. The attributes are compressed into a finite codebook during quantization, while the target item remains undetermined during decoding and its features cannot be looked up. This target-side feature vacuum weakens generation at each semantic-ID level through high conditional entropy and cascading errors, and final ranking through missing target-side feature crossing. Existing methods interact with candidate representations or generate discrete attribute tokens, but none reconstructs a continuous target-side representation inside decoding to support both stepwise generation and ranking. We propose TacGR (Stepwise Target-Side Feature Anticipation and Crossing for Generative Recommendation). Before decoding each codeword, TacGR anticipates a continuous target-side feature vector and crosses it with the semantic prefix and user behavior sequence inside the decoder. The crossed representation conditions current-level generation and is directly used for ranking. Continuous-vector regression risks a learnable target collapsing with its prediction and prediction noise propagating into generation through attention. TacGR addresses these challenges with a semantic-anchoring auxiliary tower and a unidirectional visibility mask, respectively. For extremely long industrial behavior histories, it introduces gated convolutional denoising to suppress noise and adapts the pyramid memory funnel to reduce inference cost. Offline experiments on a large-scale Lazada dataset show significant gains over OneRec, UniRec, and UniSGR. Online A/B testing improves IPV, Order, and GMV by 0.79%, 5.55%, and 3.09%, respectively.

title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.

title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
abstract: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of one memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM (commercial SRAM-CAM) and PyVaCoAl (DRAM-CAM).In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl a directed acyclic graph (DAG) reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue mode) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating collisions (Don't Care mode) yields a path-integrated confidence, CR$_2$, that silently favours direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity is a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only in a regime where it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding, the Identikit as role-filler composition, recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as attending to his fingers can make Polanyi's pianist falter, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this but narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell contingent from regime-bound tacitness. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Terence Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results whose route no one can follow and that no one yet understands well enough to extend, teach or judge. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Testable predictions follow.

title: A Generalized Elephant Random Walk with Time-Dependent Memory
abstract: The elephant random walk (ERW) is a discrete-time random walk with complete memory . At every step the walker chooses one of the previous increments at random and then either repeats with a constant probability $p\in [0,1]$ or reverses it. Since its introduction by Schütz and Trimper, the model has become a useful probabilistic framework for studying long-range dependence, anomalous diffusion, reinforcement, and phase transitions. This paper proposes a generalized ERW model with time-dependent memory . In this generalized model, the usual constant memory parameter $p$ in the standard ERW is allowed to change with time. The cental limit theorems, and the law of the iterated logarithm and some other strong laws are obtained.

title: A Nonlinear Time-Series Theory for Constant-step SGD with Momentum
abstract: Constant-step stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) augments the parameter recursion with a momentum state that carries geometrically decaying memory of past stochastic gradients. We study this coupled recursion as a nonlinear time series and develop a framework for its stationary behavior and distributional limits. The joint parameter-momentum process forgets its initialization geometrically under a finite $p$th moment for $p > 1$, yielding a unique stationary causal solution. Under a second-moment condition, this contraction leads to an invariance principle and quenched Gaussian limit for averaged SGDM, while a small-learning-rate analysis gives a Gaussian limit for the last iterate. In a stochastic-curvature quadratic model, we further study how the rate of initialization forgetting relates to stationary variance and averaged fluctuations.

title: Limit Theory for Online Expectile Estimation under Short and Long Range Dependence
abstract: Expectiles are tail-sensitive distributional summaries with important applications in financial risk measurement and forecasting, yet statistical theory for their online estimation from dependent data remains limited. We study a one-pass, stochastic-gradient algorithm with constant learning rate $γ$ for estimating the marginal expectile of a stationary causal process. The recursion admits a unique stationary causal solution and geometrically forgets its initialization. Under short-range dependence, its last iterate is asymptotically Gaussian at the $\sqrtγ$ scale, with variance governed by the population curvature and the long-run variance of the expectile score. For long- memory linear processes the scale changes to $γ^{β-1/2}\ell(1/γ)$, with a Gaussian limit arising from a fractional Brownian motion integral. We further derive the joint long- memory limit for multiple expectile levels and characterize its limiting covariance structure. Various numerical experiments corroborate the predicted Gaussian approximations and regime-specific fluctuation scales.

title: PAIR: Memory -Efficient and Fast Inference with Reading--Reasoning Fusion
abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory . At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy- memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.

title: Scalable Exact Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models-such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation-are often approximated using Pauli Twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce inaccuracies. To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by merging equivalent non-Pauli sites in the quantum circuit. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot. QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $100\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $166\times$--$1331\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory under coherent $R_Z$ noise as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-negligible and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule. QuasiStim will be open-sourced upon publication at https://github.com/isaachyw/QuasiStim

title: An Adjoint Krylov Approach to Parameter Inference for Affine Families of Linear Evolution Equations
abstract: This paper introduces an adjoint Krylov method for parameter inference in large, sparse linear evolution equations whose system matrices depend affinely on unknown coefficients. We estimate these coefficients from discrete observations by constructing one forward and one adjoint Krylov approximation on each observation interval. Quadrature of the resulting bilinear form gives the full coefficient gradient through sparse matrix-vector products, without evaluating a separate Frechet derivative in every operator direction. We separate the gradient error into forward, adjoint, and quadrature terms and derive residual-based bounds for Markov and Lindblad generators. We also identify cases in which heuristic stopping estimates become small before the gradient has converged. With workspace reuse, we compute library gradients for a 12-qubit Lindblad generator with dimension 1.7 x 10^7 on a single machine with 16 GB of memory . Experiments on chemical master, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Lindblad equations demonstrate accurate gradients and parameter recovery.

title: When Trackers Fail: VLM-Guided Verification and Recovery for Robust Video Object Segmentation
abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory . However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. title: Engram Injection: A Study of Temporal Validity in Parametric Language-Model Memory
abstract: A stored fact may stop being valid when a user changes a preference or an event replaces an earlier one. We study whether a language model can learn these changes in its parameters and answer correctly from only a question and the current time. Engram Injection stores facts in LoRA adapters and supplies the clock through FiLM conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model. We compare it with additive clock conditioning, prompting with the full dated history, and retrieving four dated records. We train six matched adapters across three seeds after fixing a sampler that could admit test-age examples into training. The training audit reports no such examples among 127,760 evaluated training inputs. On 62 pairs of questions asked before and after an update, at an elapsed age of seven days excluded from training, both adapter methods answer zero pairs correctly under the primary blinded assistant review with order code 1 held fixed. Full-history prompting answers 59/62 pairs correctly, and retrieval answers 62/62. Separate experiments show that adapters can store facts and that removable memory units can support local deletion. Combining fact selection with time-based version selection remains unsuccessful. These results separate learning a fact from learning when to use it.

title: End-to-End Fidelity and Rate Analysis for Zero-Added-Loss Multiplexing
abstract: Zero-added-loss multiplexing (ZALM)~[Phys. Rev. Appl. {\bf 19}, 054029 (2023)] is a midpoint-source scheme for entanglement distribution. Its quantum transmitter (QTX) employs two Sagnac sources of polarization-entangled pairs plus partial Bell-state measurements (BSMs) on their idler outputs to herald entanglement in their signal outputs, thus avoiding the switching losses suffered by other multiplexing approaches. When its Sagnac sources' spontaneous parametric downconverters (SPDCs) utilize $χ^{(2)}$ crystals with phase-matched spectral islands, ZALM avoids the tradeoff between heralding efficiency and output-state fidelity incurred when conventional-crystal SPDCs' outputs are channelized by dense wavelength-division multiplexing filters. This paper reports an end-to-end fidelity and rate analysis for islands-based ZALM that includes: SPDC multipair emissions of all orders and partial-BSM losses in the ZALM QTX; loss in propagation from the ZALM QTX to Alice and Bob's quantum receivers (QRXs); loss and mode mismatch in the mode converters employed at Alice and Bob's QRXs; and loss in the partial-BSM loading of Alice and Bob's emissive quantum memories .

title: Integration, Enhancements and Evaluation of Memory Simulators
abstract: Currently, there is no common methodology or set of practices for evaluating memory -system performance in integrated simulation infrastructures. As a result, studies adopt different evaluation approaches, which can lead to conflicting conclusions even for the same simulation infrastructure. We propose a validation methodology that evaluates memory -system performance from three complementary views: the memory simulator, the CPU-- memory interface and the simulated application. We use these views to detect, understand and correct memory -simulation inaccuracies arising from simulator integration and simplified modeling of microarchitectural features. The methodology reveals that the application's perception of memory performance can become effectively decoupled from the detailed memory simulation. Most importantly, we identify and correct a fundamental memory -model mismatch between delayed-response cycle-accurate memory simulators and ZSim, a representative parallel CPU simulator. title: Totem: Object-Centric 3D Memory for World-Consistent Video Generation
abstract: Generating coherent videos grounded in a unified underlying world remains a major challenge, particularly under large viewpoint changes, where existing methods often struggle to maintain stable representations of individual objects. To this end, we introduce Totem, an object-centric 3D memory framework for world-consistent video generation. Totem first represents each selected object as a persistent 3D memory aligned to a shared world frame, assigning it a dedicated state. Based on these memories , we design a dual-stream 3D conditioning architecture that combines object memories with scene geometry for target-view synthesis. Moreover, these object memories constrain the model's attention with 3D structural information, thereby preserving object surfaces and relative spatial layouts. Extensive experiments on world-generation and object-centric benchmarks demonstrate that Totem generates videos depicting a more object-consistent 3D world under challenging camera trajectories, while supporting versatile applications.

title: Reference-Efficient Multimodal Bitstream-Corrupted Video Recovery via Depth-Conditioned Adaptation
abstract: Recovering visually faithful content from damaged video bitstreams is important for reliable multimedia communication and storage. Existing methods exploit local residuals and non-local RGB references of the input video sequence, but both sources can become unreliable after decoding, while processing additional references increases receiver computation and memory . This paper studies multimodal bitstream-corrupted video recovery (MBSCVR) using RGB and depth information, where pre-transmission depth-based geometry aids reconstruction when the received appearance is corrupted. We propose a novel MBSCVR framework that selects and effectively utilizes a single selected non-local RGB reference per recovery window to achieve higher performance. It integrates a reliability-aware multimodal selector that combines valid appearance with depth compatibility before reference encoding. Depth-Conditioned Reference Adaptation (DCRA) introduces selected RGB evidence into feature completion and content generation, while frame-aligned depth conditions completion queries. On the complete BSCV benchmark with oracle masks, MBSCVR uses one selected reference to achieve 32.30 dB on YouTube-VOS and 28.93 dB on DAVIS, surpassing full-reference B2SCVR by 0.27 and 0.33 dB and improving SSIM on both subsets. Matched receiver-forward measurements show 36.8\% lower latency and 40.8\% lower peak memory . These results demonstrate how compact geometric guidance and adapted appearance processing improve the quality--resource trade-off of multimedia recovery.

title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.

title: Native Dual Pools or Shared Paging? Memory Organization for Concurrent Hybrid LLM Serving
abstract: Hybrid attention-SSM serving combines growing attention KV with fixed-size recurrent and convolution state whose allocation units, reuse boundaries, and lifetimes differ. We implement four memory organizations in a modified vLLM runtime: a coarse shared-page baseline (S0), checkpoint-internal recurrent paging (S1), paging with convolution-slot packing (S2), and native dual pools (D0). Nine evaluation questions cover storage costs and serving behavior. The cumulative S0-S1-S2 refinement improves completed-output throughput and tail completion time at the main operating point. D0-S2 performance varies with memory budget, offered load, and admission headroom. Shared-prefix workloads yield larger stepwise gains; gains also persist in a no-sharing control with equal recorded input-work totals. State traces identify recurrent-checkpoint availability as the limit on joint reuse in the tested S2 runs. Extending producer-side checkpoint lifetime increases reusable depth at a fixed page budget. A fresh-seed SHARE/ISOLATE comparison estimates a positive retention interaction, with a primary confidence interval that includes zero. Retained-state continuation correctness remains unresolved. These findings motivate evaluating physical state representation together with request admission and checkpoint lifetime when designing memory management for concurrent hybrid-model serving.

title: RSAJEV: Training-Free Abstaining Prototype Memory for Eliminating Silent Hallucination in JEV-Based Remote Sensing Classification
abstract: Scene classification of remote sensing imagery with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is formulated as a single-forward-pass decision problem: candidate class names are lettered options in the prompt, a registered answer slot is conditioned on the prompt, and classification is read out by scoring letter tokens with the language-modeling head. We show that although this letter binding is highly effective within its training vocabulary (97.71% OA on UCM), it behaves erratically out of vocabulary: zero-adaptation accuracy across four cross-dataset directions fluctuates between 7.35% and 96.40%, and under out-of-vocabulary weights its confidence fails inversely on open-set evaluation, assigning higher confidence to unseen than to seen classes (AUROC 0.38), a failure we term silent hallucination. We retain the slot representation and replace the readout with RSAJEV, a training-free abstaining prototype memory that performs retrieval-based prototype matching: K reference images per class are cached as prototypes via their slot representations under the same prompt, and classification becomes nearest-neighbor retrieval over the prototypes, refined by a shrinkage-Mahalanobis geometric correction. This readout is mechanistically isomorphic to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) but operates on discriminative decisions; it is the first retrieval-based readout for MLLM slot representations. The retrieval readout reaches 89.43% on the UCM cross-dataset gate with 16 references per class and zero gradient updates, and 96.90% on AID. Its ID-ness scores attain 0.91-0.99 AUROC on open-set evaluation over two datasets, exceeding symbolic confidence (0.38-0.96) in all four open-set settings, restoring a calibratable abstention channel and supporting class addition/removal at zero extra inference cost via offline rescoring of the cached matrix.

title: A Dependency-Aware Multi-GPU Training Framework for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) achieve superior performance in many dynamic graph learning tasks. These models use node state vectors (i.e., memories ) to capture and record graph changes (i.e., events), and then exploit these memories to assist prediction. However, this memory -centric design makes multi-GPU training challenging because predictions for later events often depend on memory updates from earlier events. To maintain model quality, existing multi-GPU TGNN training schemes strictly preserve all event dependencies, which limits parallelism and causes expensive cross-GPU memory synchronization. In this work, we observe that many of these dependencies can be handled more flexibly without harming training quality. Specifically, (a) dependencies in TGNN training have high locality in both time and graph topology, (b) the short-range dependencies missed within a large batch can often be recovered cheaply, and (c) many memory updates are not immediately needed. Based on these observations, we propose DepBloom to accelerate multi-GPU TGNN training with three techniques: (1) temporally bounded spatial partitioning to reduce unnecessary cross-GPU synchronization and improve parallelism; (2) intra-batch memory refinement to recover missing short-range temporal dependencies inside enlarged batches; and (3) critical-path optimization to prioritize urgent memory updates while deferring non-critical work during multi-GPU pipeline execution. Experimental results across representative models and diverse datasets show that DepBloom achieves an average speedup of 2.84$\times$ and up to 5.16$\times$ over state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining comparable or better model accuracy.

title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.

title: Suggested Is Not Superseded: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of a System-One Model as a Memory-Retirement Gate
abstract: Long-term memory for assistants needs a gate that decides when a new utterance retires an old stored claim. Benchmark labels for this step mark a pair as changed or not, so they cannot tell a gate that acts on established change from one that acts on a hint. We write a task contract that separates the two (SUPERSEDED vs. NEEDS-CONFIRMATION vs. COMPATIBLE), label 500 test pairs built from STALE (change pairs plus same-user controls) with three LLM annotators and two human adjudicators (one author and a second annotator; provenance reported), and evaluate Jev, a typed "System One" decision model, under pre-registered hypotheses. Of the 179 test pairs STALE marks as changed, 72 meet the contract's bar for an established change. Jev never retired a claim on 141 same-conversation non-changes. Its failure is premature retirement: the binary gate retires 39.2% of claims whose change is only suggested. A three-way decision cuts this to 15.5% at a 15.3-point detection cost, which misses our pre-registered 10-point budget, and it lands on the binary gate's own threshold frontier; these verdicts hold under three readings of the gold labels. On a held-out vault scored against a second annotator's labels, a cascade that escalated uncertain cases to a reasoning model and looked best on development data was indistinguishable from simply raising the threshold (premature retirement 26.8% vs. 6.5% on dev). Part of the gap comes from the gold labels: relative to that annotator's reading, LLM-majority gold shares most of its errors with a same-family escalation model, and an identity for binary labels says how much such shared errors hide. The rest is small-sample selection on development data. For builders this means a binary score should not be wired to delete: route suggested changes to pending evidence, and do not trust a cascade selected on development data of this size.

title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.

title: Developing the Statistical Mechanics of Evolving Assembly Spaces
abstract: A gap exists in connecting biological evolution within the framework of statistical mechanics. It has been hoped that statistical mechanics would provide us with a general predictive principle for the emergence of novelty and complexity. However, the emergence of novel functional features initiated by stochastic processes remains difficult to describe, because these processes commonly arise outside near-equilibrium or linear-response regimes. To understand how environmental influences generate diverse, open-ended, complex objects by driving physical systems to specific regions of phase space over long spatial and temporal scales, a new approach to non-equilibrium thermodynamics is necessary. Here, we present the coupling of assembly theory (AT) with statistical mechanics as a framework that works within the laws of thermodynamics, but can contextualise the processes of novelty, complexity, and evolution within these laws. We map construction processes from physical space to assembly space (AS) and introduce the concept of an assembler, a machine that constructs objects contingent on previous states and is represented by bitwise operations. Using this approach, we apply principles from stochastic thermodynamics with AT to define selection within large combinatorial spaces1 and estimate the work required to create novel and complex objects. This approach allows us to represent complex processes, such as selection, within large combinatorial spaces as a set of rules for a memory -feedback loop followed by the assembler. This framework concretely defines the relationships between thermodynamics and information theory by introducing a novel aspect of physics that uses history and causal contingency to influence the probabilistic time evolution of complex systems.

title: FARL: A Fully Automated Pipeline of RL Interface and Solver Design
abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) largely focuses on optimizing learning algorithms within a pre-defined task formulation, while applying RL to new tasks still relies heavily on human expertise to design the learning pipeline: what an agent observes, how it is rewarded, which algorithm it uses, and how training is configured. Automating these choices is challenging because they are tightly coupled. We introduce FARL (Fully Automated Reinforcement Learning), a framework that automates RL design by jointly searching observation and reward programs, learning algorithms, and training settings. FARL uses training statistics and observed behavior to diagnose failures, propose changes, and test whether they improve learning. Its search preserves diverse candidates and the controls needed for these tests, using a staged budget to screen designs before investing in longer training. Experimental memory records each finding together with its conditions, so an unsuccessful component can be reconsidered in a different combination. Across expert-withheld and expert-available settings, FARL outperforms the evaluated automated baselines on challenging navigation, locomotion, and manipulation tasks. On Adroit Hand Relocate, FARL achieves 97.1% success at 5M training steps per policy, compared with 0% for Eureka and LiMEN and 1.0% for native Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) under the same policy training budget.

title: Recovering Low-Bit Failures in Vision-Language-Action Policies via Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantization lowers deployment costs of vision-language-action (VLA) policies but can compromise task completion. Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, we systematically reveal that quantization-aware training (QAT) generally improves on post-training quantization (PTQ) but leaves substantial gaps to full precision (FP) on long-horizon tasks and under visual and semantic shifts, while its imitation-based objective does not explicitly use rollout success or partial completion. To exploit these outcome signals, we introduce Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (QCRL), an offline RL method coupling progress-based advantage estimation with quantization-aware source conditioning. FP rollouts supply reference experience beyond action-level distillation, progress-scaled terminal penalty distinguishes partial completion, and quantization-aware conditioning selects advantageous reference behavior within the quantized policy. We evaluate weight-only INT4 W4A16 on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 and joint weight-activation NVFP4 W4A4 on $π_{0.5}$. Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP's mean score across three visual-shift conditions for $π_{0.5}$ with INT4 W4A16, alongside 42.9% model- memory savings. With NVFP4 W4A4, it reaches 100.7% of the same FP baseline, alongside a $1.73\times$ speedup using NVFP4/FP8 deployment. Hardware gains are relative to FP16 on Jetson Thor.
